FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Compare indications and contraindications for elbow arthroscopy.
Assess and implement appropriate patient positioning and limb preparation.
Select appropriate portal placement and arthroscopy technique.
Identify procedural pitfalls and possible complications.
Procedure
Indications
The use of elbow arthroscopy is increasing in all age groups, including new ventures into
arthroscopic fracture fixation and ulnohumeral arthroplasty.




Indications in younger patients may include valgus extension overload, osteophyte complex,
osteochondritis dissecans of the capitellum, chondral lesions, and loose-body removal.
Indications in older patients include arthritis (inflammatory/rheumatoid, osteoarthritic,
posttraumatic, septic, hemophilic); lateral epicondylitis; elbow contracture/adhesions; synovial
processes; loose-body removal; plica; trochlear chondromalacia; impingement; arthrofibrosis;
and arthroscopic-assisted fracture fixation of the radial head, coronoid, or capitellum.1,2

Indications
The indications for elbow arthroscopy in orthopaedics are increasing. This has grown to
include:
1. The evaluation and débridement of arthritic changes, including osteophytes from the
olecranon process, the coronoid, and the trochlea
2. Postoperative or posttraumatic lysis of adhesions and release of capsular contractions
3. Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) débridement and release of the extensor carpi
radialis brevis
4. Capitellar osteochondritis dissecans screw fixation, débridement, fragment excision,
microfracture, or osteochondral transplant procedures
5. Irrigation and débridement of septic arthritis
6. Arthroscopic synovectomy of rheumatoid arthritis
7. Removal of loose bodies
8. Resection of pathologic radiocapitellar plica
9. Débridement of olecranon bursitis
10. Radial head excision
11. Arthroscopic-assisted fracture fixation
12. As a diagnostic examination for patients with a persistently painful elbow and
inconclusive examination findings2,3 (Resource 1).
Contraindications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
2/23

Soft-tissue contraindications, such as local infection, burns, joint contractures, and elbow
instability
Osseous contraindications, such as bony ankylosis/heterotopic ossification, prior intra-
articular elbow trauma, advanced arthritis changes
Prior intra-articular elbow open surgery may cause nerves to scar in unpredictable locations
and scar to the joint capsule, putting them at risk. Ulnar nerve transposition is not an absolute
contraindication but necessitates careful examination to identify the location of the nerve.

Contraindications
Alterations to normal anatomy make minimally invasive or percutaneous procedures
technically challenging and, in many patients, unsafe. This also is true for arthroscopic
elbow procedures. Any anatomic distortion that would alter the paths of the
neurovascular structures and make portal insertion unsafe should not be undertaken.4
These include superficial skin burns/scarring, soft tissue/joint contractures, or variations
in normal osseous articulations caused by prior trauma. In addition, a main preoperative
consideration is prior cubital tunnel release with ulnar nerve transposition. If present,
the medial portals cannot be safely placed without identifying the exact path of the ulnar
nerve; this can be done via ultrasonography or MRI. Ulnar nerve subluxation does not
prohibit arthroscopy; however, identification of the ulnar nerve and maintenance of its
reduction within the cubital tunnel for the duration of the procedure are imperative.
Lastly, several specific procedures previously have been considered for arthroscopy that
are best undertaken via an open approach. These include medial epicondylitis
débridement, secondary to its proximity to the ulnar nerve, and collateral ligament
repair, because of its insufficient exposure of ligament origin/insertion and cubital/radial
tunnel nerve decompression.
Techniques
Preoperative Planning
Obtain a complete patient history, perform a complete physical examination, and review
appropriate radiographic imaging studies with the patient.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
3/23

Obtain appropriate imaging studies. A CT scan may be obtained to improve visualization of
intra-articular fractures, osteoarthritis, or loose bodies, and MRI may be obtained to identify
osteochondral defects, synovial lesions, or ligamentous/capsular disruption.
Evaluate for concomitant upper extremity injuries or joint mobility limitations that may restrict
prone or lateral decubitus positioning.
Document status of major peripheral nerves and obtain preoperative electromyography/nerve
conduction velocity tests if any pre-existing compressive neuropathies are suspected.
Review and understand the course of surrounding neurovascular structures as they traverse
the elbow joint.
Consider factors such as the acuity of the injury (elbow effusion/scar tissue), elbow
ligamentous instability, and anticoagulated/hemophilic states, all of which may increase the
difficulty of elbow arthroscopy and should be incorporated into planning.

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative planning begins with a complete patient history and physical examination.
This should include obtaining preoperative pain scores and assessing elbow, shoulder,
and wrist range of motion. The patient’s specific complaint (pain, stiffness, instability,
weakness) and the goals of treatment should be documented and discussed. These
factors must be considered in selecting a procedure and in developing realistic
postoperative expectations. In addition, all attempts should be made to provide a
definitive diagnosis before offering arthroscopic treatment. Diagnostic arthroscopy
should be the last course of action. For most of the already mentioned indications, the
physician should attempt nonsurgical management via NSAIDs, activity modifications,
and physical therapy before offering surgical treatment. However, if nonsurgical
treatment has failed and the patient continues to have functional impairment, pain, or
both, elbow arthroscopy may be a very successful surgical option if preoperative
planning is executed successfully. In the context of more involved surgical procedures,
the possibility of conversion to an open procedure should be discussed with the patient.
On the day of surgery, patient positioning and potential administration of a regional
nerve block should be discussed and agreed on with the anesthesiologist. The
appropriate surgical table, table attachments (arm boards, arm bolsters), positioning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
4/23

accessories (bean bag, chest rolls, arm bump, axillary roll), and arthroscopy equipment
(monitor; light/camera control box; low-flow, low-pressure pump; irrigation bags;
arthroscopes; arthroscopic shaver/burr; radiofrequency ablation; cannulas; and
arthroscopic instrument trays) should be confirmed before intubation. Finally, the
planned sequence of portal placement and instrumentation should be discussed with
the surgical team to maximize efficiency and thereby decrease the risk of fluid
extravasation and nerve injury.
Patient Positioning
Prone: The patient is positioned chest down with the shoulder at the edge of the bed. The
elbow is flexed over an arm board aligned parallel to the bed or an arm holder, with the
forearm in the dependent position.
Lateral decubitus: A beanbag or well-padded peg board positions the patient on his or her side
with the shoulder flexed forward. The elbow is stabilized over a bed-attachment post or arm
holder (Figure 1).
Supine cross-body: An arm-holding device or an assistant holds the arm across the chest.
Supine suspension: The arm is suspended vertically in abduction via means of a traction
suspensory device.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
5/23

Figure 1 Intraoperative photograph shows lateral decubitus positioning with the use of a bean
bag for stability and an arm bolster to secure the surgical limb. A pneumatic tourniquet is
placed proximally on the upper arm. Courtesy of Sean M. Mitchell, MD, Orlando, FL. 

Patient Positioning
Surgical positioning is an important preoperative consideration for elbow arthroscopy.
Several factors should be considered in deciding among supine, lateral decubitus, or
prone positioning. Ipsilateral injuries, shoulder or elbow contractures, body habitus, or
concerns regarding anesthesia may preclude a patient from certain positioning. The
lateral and prone positions allow the surgical arm to rest on a holder or post, providing
stability to the extremity. Supine positions involve resting the arm on the chest or
requires a traction device to suspend the arm vertically and are inherently less stable.
Without stability, unexpected withdrawal of instruments from the portals may occur as
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
6/23

the arm shifts or sways. In addition, the supine suspension position introduces difficulty
in accessing the posterior compartment because the instruments will be in a near-
vertical orientation. The disadvantages of the lateral decubitus and prone positions are
the need to reposition the patient, which increases surgical time and is associated with
potential difficulties in anesthetic management. In patients with a shorter upper
extremity (eg, those who are young or have a rhizomelic abnormality), the arm holder
will limit elbow access. The prone and lateral decubitus positions are most commonly
used for elbow arthroscopy.
Limb Preparation
Regardless of patient positioning, the tourniquet should be as proximal on the arm as possible
to allow for unobstructed portal placement and working space.
With the patient in the lateral or prone position, ensure that the arm holder or post is as
proximal as possible.
Use a compressive dressing over the forearm to prevent fluid extravasation.
Before instrument insertion, insufflate the elbow joint through the lateral portal (soft spot)
before placing portals. This will displace neurovascular structures away from the joint and
facilitate trocar introduction.

Limb Preparation
After administration of general anesthesia, the arm should be positioned over the edge
of the surgical table, positioned over a bed-attachment arm bolster, or affixed to a
suspension device, depending on patient positioning. If the patient is in the lateral
decubitus position, the patient or the surgical bed should be tilted toward the surgeon
so the limb does not slide away during the procedure, leaving the arm bolster to creep
into the antecubital fossa. In each patient, the goal is to provide access to the entire
extremity. Similarly, sterile preparation and draping should include the shoulder to
afford maximal exposure. Apply a sterile stockinette from the hand to the proximal
forearm, distal to the radial head, and secure it tightly with self-adhesive wrap. This
compressive wrap also will limit fluid extravasation into the subcutaneous tissue and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
7/23

muscle compartments of the forearm. A sterile tourniquet should then be applied, and
the limb should be exsanguinated.
After the limb has been positioned and draped, anatomic structures should be outlined
appropriately. Moving from medial to lateral, encircle the medial epicondyle, palpate and
outline the course of the ulnar nerve, mark the proximal edge of the olecranon process,
mark the lateral border of the triceps muscle, encircle the lateral epicondyle, and trace
the radiocapitellar joint. Next, mark the proposed anteromedial, anterolateral, and
posterior portals (Video 1).
Video 1 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Essential Anatomy and Portal Markings. Columbus,
OH, 2022
Before portal insertion, the joint must be insufflated. This makes trocar penetration into
the capsule easier and also displaces neurovascular structures from the joint. The lateral
epicondyle, the olecranon, and the radial head form three points of a triangle, at the
center of which lies the appropriate position for the direct lateral portal or soft spot.
Because this portal is a safe location away from neurovascular structures, it is used for
initial joint insufflation. Insert an 18-gauge spinal needle into the joint capsule and, using
connection tubing, attach the needle to a 60-mL syringe filled with sterile normal saline.
The joint is insufflated with 20 to 40 mL of sterile saline (Video 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
8/23

Video 2 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Elbow Joint Insufflation Technique. Columbus, OH,
2022.
Surgical Approaches
Arthroscopy Portals 5-10
Medial portals
Proximal anteromedial (superomedial) portal: 2 cm proximal to the medial epicondyle and
immediately anterior to the intermuscular septum, approximately 1 cm anterior to the
anterior humerus
Safest and most commonly used medial portal
Mid-anteromedial portal: 1 cm proximal and 1 cm anterior to the medial epicondyle
Distal (standard) anteromedial portal: 2 cm distal and 2 cm anterior to the medial epicondyle
No longer the primary portal; used as an accessory portal for retractors
Lateral portals
Proximal anterolateral portal: 2 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle and immediately
anterior to the intermuscular septum, approximately 1 cm anterior to the humerus
Safest and most used lateral portal
Mid-anterolateral portal: immediately proximal and anterior to the radiocapitellar joint
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
9/23

Distal anterolateral portal: 2 to 3 cm distal and 1 cm anterior to the lateral epicondyle above
the sulcus of the radiocapitellar joint
Direct lateral portal: at the center of a triangle outlined by the olecranon, the lateral
epicondyle, and the radial head; the initial portal for joint insufflation and for access to the
lateral gutter and the radiocapitellar joint
Posterior portals
Direct (straight) posterior portal: 3 cm proximal to the tip of the olecranon; the main
posterior working portal
Posterolateral portal: 3 cm proximal to the olecranon off the lateral edge of the triceps; the
main posterior viewing portal
Techniques
Portal Placement 3,7,10
The order of portal placement is determined by the elbow pathology and surgeon preference;
however, each portal should be created via a nick-and-spread technique down to the joint
capsule, at which a blunt trocar should be used to penetrate the capsule.
The safest position for anterior portal placement and the one that facilitates improved
instrument navigation is with the elbow flexed at 90°. The opposite is true for the posterior
elbow, which should be approached in extension.
In deciding placement of medial or lateral portals for the anterior side of the elbow joint, the
more proximal locations are closer to bone and further from traversing nerves (Figure
2; Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
10/23

Figure 2 Illustrations show the location of the anterior portals used in arthroscopic surgery of
the elbow. A, Lateral view of the elbow. The proximal anterolateral, anterolateral, and
midlateral (soft spot) portals are shown in relation to the radial nerve. B, Medial view of the
elbow. The anteromedial and proximal anteromedial portals are shown in relation to the
median, ulnar, and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves. (Reproduced from Yamaguchi K,
Tashjian RZ: Setup and portals, in Yamaguchi K, King GJW, McKee MD, O’Driscoll SWM, eds:
Advanced Reconstruction: Elbow. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2007, pp 3-11.)

Portal Placement
As the surgeon creates anterior portals, a superficial incision is established through the
dermal layer only, followed by blunt dissection with a hemostat to the level of the joint
capsule to decrease the risk of neurovascular damage.11 A blunt trocar should then be
used to pass through into the joint because the use of sharp trocars increases the rate of
injury to surrounding nerves. This is best done with the elbow flexed, which increases
anterior joint space and displaces the nervous structures from the joint. Stothers et al8
demonstrated the importance of elbow flexion during portal placement, showing that
the mean distance from the portal sheath to the adjacent nerve increases from
extension to flexion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
11/23

This establishes an initial viewing portal. At this stage, diagnostic arthroscopy of the
anterior compartment can be performed. Evaluation should include inspection of the
radiocapitellar and ulnohumeral articulations and examination for signs of underlying
arthritic changes. Next, an evaluation for chondral wear, soft-tissue flaps, loose bodies,
and/or extensor carpi radialis brevis degeneration should be performed. The case
presentation of a patient with lateral epicondylitis is reviewed in (Video 3) to show this
initial step and serve as an example for the appropriate progression of elbow
arthroscopy. The second portal will function as a working portal. This portal should be
placed under direct visualization via the outside-in technique. An 18-gauge spinal needle
can be introduced to identify proper portal entry site and angle (Video 4). After the
portal is placed, a shaver is introduced to débride synovial tissue for improved
visualization. After visualization is appropriate, débridement of arthritic changes,
chondral wear, soft-tissue flaps, or pathologic extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon be
performed (Videos 5 and 6). Because several nerves travel in close proximity to the
anterior and posteromedial joint capsule, it is important to use suction on the shaver
sparingly. An accessory portal and the use of a capsular retractor may be considered to
improve visualization and working space. In general, the order of events once inside the
joint are diagnostic arthroscopy, bony procedures, loose body removal, and capsular
work. After the capsule is violated, the rate of fluid extravasation increases.
Video 3 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Lateral Epicondylitis Case Presentation and Anterior
Compartment Diagnostic Arthroscopy. Columbus, OH, 2022.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
12/23

Video 4 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Anterolateral Portal Placement. Columbus, OH,
2022.
Video 5 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Anterolateral Portal Shaver Introduction and
Débridement. Columbus, OH, 2022.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
13/23

Video 6 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Post-débridement of the Extensor Carpi Radialis
Brevis, Lateral Elbow Anatomy Review. Columbus, OH, 2022.
Posteriorly, portal placement is relatively safe because of the distance from local nerves.
The posterolateral portal is used mainly as a viewing portal, whereas the direct posterior
portal is the main working portal. The thick triceps tendon will need to be penetrated
during establishment of the direct posterior portal. Therefore, a deeper stab incision,
nearly down to bone, can be used for this portal insertion. This technique is safe for this
portal only. Similar to the anterior compartment, initial débridement of the posterior fat
pad should be performed to improve visualization, specifically in the olecranon fossa
(Video 7). Next, evaluation of the olecranon tip, of the ulnohumeral joint, of the
posterolateral and posteromedial gutters for osteophytes, and for loose bodies should
be performed. Caution should be exercised if working in the posteromedial gutter
because the ulnar nerve traverses over this structure (Video 8).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
14/23

Video 7 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Posterior Compartment Portal Placement.
Columbus, OH, 2022.
Video 8 Awan H, Mitchell SM: Video. Posterior Compartment Débridement and
Diagnostic Arthroscopy. Columbus, OH, 2022.
Postoperative Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
15/23

Specific postoperative management recommendations depend on the pathology and the
procedures being performed.
A general principle to follow is that the elbow joint should not be immobilized more than a few
days postoperatively, and gentle, early range of motion exercises should be encouraged.
The use of continuous passive motion machines and indomethacin for heterotopic ossification
prophylaxis are controversial.

Postoperative Management
Wounds are closed with the use of simple sutures. A small gauze dressing should be
placed over the portal sites, and a compressive dressing should be applied from the
hand to the middle arm to alleviate swelling. Application of a sling, hinged elbow brace,
or splint depends on the procedure performed; however, in general, early range of
motion will help prevent stiffness of contractures. Postoperative care and rehabilitation
protocols are procedure- and surgeon-specific.
After diagnostic arthroscopy, synovectomy, resection of pathologic plica, arthroscopic
bursectomy, osteophyte débridement, or loose body removal, a soft compressive
dressing and shoulder sling are applied for postoperative comfort. Gentle, early elbow
range of motion exercises are encouraged in the immediate postoperative period, with
return to activities and weight bearing as tolerated after wounds have healed and
swelling has decreased. This usually occurs 2 weeks postoperatively. After 4 weeks,
patients can return to athletics, strength training, and heavy labor.
After capsular contracture releases, lysis of adhesions for arthrofibrosis, or débridement
and extensor carpi radialis brevis release for tennis elbow, brief postoperative splint
immobilization can be used from 1 day to 1 week postoperatively. These procedures
should be followed by aggressive physical therapy immediately after the splint is
removed. The use of continuous passive motion machines is common but not supported
by the literature. For patients with prior postoperative adhesions, contracture, or ectopic
bone formation, prophylaxis for heterotopic ossification via indomethacin can be
initiated; however, the efficacy of such prophylaxis is controversial.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
16/23

Management of osteochondritis dissecans or arthroscopic-assisted fracture fixation will
require a brief 1- to 2-week period of immobilization followed by protected range of
motion in a brace. Physical therapy can be provided as necessary for postoperative
stiffness. Strengthening should not begin until swelling and stiffness have subsided and
the patient can obtain near full range of motion, approximately 6 weeks postoperatively
(and no earlier).
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Under insufflating the joint may cause extracapsular portal placement and risk nerve damage.
Use the fewest number of portals necessary and manage fluid pressure to prevent
extravasation, which may obstruct elbow motion and alter elbow anatomy.12
The use of shaver suction or radiofrequency ablation increases the risk of nerve damage.
Ensure the ulnar nerve is protected with retractors and instrument suction is off when working
on the posteromedial elbow to avoid damage to this structure.
Regional blocks will prevent postoperative neurovascular examination and should not be used
in patients with pre-existing neuropathy.

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Maintaining a portal after a trocar is inserted and preventing reinsertion attempts is
essential to preventing iatrogenic nerve injuries. This can be completed by placing
portals under direct visualization and by incorporating interchangeable cannulas, rubber
diaphragms, and switching sticks. The use of fenestrated portals can damage nerves
during insertion and should be avoided. In addition, the use of an intracapsular suction
shaver or radiofrequency ablation has been documented as a cause of nerve damage if
used in close proximity to the capsule, especially posteromedially adjacent to the ulnar
nerve. In regard to elbow positioning, flexion decreases risk of nerve damage and
improves working space in the anterior elbow. Conversely, elbow extension improves
visualization in the posterior elbow. Lastly, to allow for the most working space around
the elbow, the tourniquet and arm holder should be placed as proximally as possible.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
17/23

Complications
Nerve injury is the most common and concerning complication. Most of these injuries are
transient nerve palsies that recover with observation.
The radial and lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerves are at risk with placement of
anterolateral portals, the median and medial antebrachial cutaneous nerves are at risk with
placement of anterolateral portals, and the ulnar nerve is at risk with placement of medial
portals and with prolonged retraction medially or prolonged joint distension.
Portal mispositioning, failure to use blunt dissection, aggressive shuttling of instruments, and
prolonged joint distension are all risk factors.
Heterotopic ossification, infection, and persistent drainage from portal sites occur less
frequently.

Complications
Nerve palsies have been documented to occur in zero to 14% of patients who undergo
elbow arthroscopy. 4, 7, 11,13-15 This is not a surprising finding given the results of a
cadaver model study that showed the frequency with which common portals came to
rest in contact with local nerves. For example, the distal anterolateral portal was found in
contact with the radial nerve and the anterior branch of the posterior antebrachial
cutaneous nerve in 56% and 43% of cases, respectively. The proximal anterolateral
portal was adjacent to the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve in 29% of cases. On
the anteromedial side, the proximal portal abutted the medial antebrachial nerve in 56%
of cases, with the distal portal abutting the anterior branch of the same nerve in 71% of
cases. 8
A retrospective study of 473 consecutive arthroscopy procedures identified 12 patients
(2.5%) with transient palsies, 5 patients (1.26%) with ulnar palsies, 4 patients (0.84%) with
radial palsies, and 3 patients (0.21%) with palsy involving the posterior interosseous,
medial antebrachial cutaneous, or anterior interosseous nerves.16 Several recent studies
also have documented the ulnar nerve as having the highest occurrence of
postoperative neuropraxia, followed by the radial nerve, followed then by only rare
occurrences in several other nerves. 16-18 Nerve transections were even more
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:02 PM
AAOS | Elbow Arthroscopy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000047
18/23

infrequent, documented mainly in case reports. 19-21 Risk factors for these nerve injuries
include rheumatoid arthritis, posttraumatic arthritis, elbow contractures, and capsular
contraction release. 14
Other complications have been reported. Postoperative intra-articular infection (zero to
0.8%), superficial surgical site infections (2.0% to 4.5%), postoperative heterotopic
ossification (2.4% to 2.5%), complex regional pain syndrome (3.4%), postsurgical
contracture (1.6%), and prolonged clear drainage from a portal site (5.0%) have been
reported in several studies. 3,16,17,22,23
Outcomes
Arthroscopy can provide minimally invasive treatment options for elbow arthritis,
contractures/adhesions, osteochondral defects, joint infection, and loose bodies, and can
serve a diagnostic option for persistent pain.23
Although elbow arthroscopy decreases postoperative pain and the risk of infection, the
literature has not shown it to be associated with a faster return to work or superior outcomes.
This technique improves visualization of pathology, aids in fracture reduction, and allows for
more complete intra-articular débridement.

Outcomes
Elbow arthroscopy is a relatively safe procedure and a less invasive treatment option for
various pathologies. Several studies have reported good outcomes in terms of improved
postoperative pain, range of motion, and functional elbow scores for various
pathologies, including arthritis, osteochondritis dissecans, and arthrofibrosis. 22, 25-27
Compared with open procedures, arthroscopy offers smaller surgical incisions,
decreased risk of infection, lower accumulation of deep or superficial scars, and lower
pain scores. 16,28-31
